source.title: Standard vs. Modular Sampling: Best Practices for Reliable LLM Unlearning
source.authors: Praveen Bushipaka; Lucia C. Passaro; Tommaso Cucinotta

page_placements.theme: Method and setting sensitivity of measured forgetting
Forgetting reached through degenerate, collapsed, fabricated or blanket-refusal output

record.file_problem: none; full paper text, including appendix, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study experimentally evaluates unlearning efficacy and utility under different data and sampling practices, using its own measures. It does not test recovery attacks, so its results bear only on the unlearning-performance portion of version A.
record.gate_note: No fine-tuning recovery attack, activation-direction ablation, quantization, or prompting-only recovery test is reported. The forget-efficacy and model-utility results are included because they directly measure the unlearning-performance and utility aspects of version A. GA is described as not implemented, so it is not recorded as an experimental result. The MMLU scores are reported as a general-utility check but are not included as separate rows because the table’s MU-T measure is the directly reported utility outcome for version A.
record.test_reason: The study compares retain-set compositions and sampling schemes, including its own MELU, for GD, DPO and NPO entity unlearning on LLaMA 3.1 8B Instruct. It reports only forget efficacy (FE) and utility on standard, non-adversarial queries. It runs no relearning, internal-edit, quantization or prompting recovery, and does no deletion-versus-hiding analysis. FE is a composite (1 minus the mean of ROUGE-L, probability and cosine), not accuracy relative to chance. So its results cannot show whether forgetting is shallow or robust, and they bear on no version as stated. Version A's claim that simple attacks don't recover the knowledge is never tested. It is T4 because it uses standard unlearning methods as tools and reports only how its own data and sampling practices (MELU) perform.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that retain-set composition matters, and they recommend a diverse mix of neighbour sets to balance forget efficacy and utility. Yet in their own Table 1 the Balanced mix is not better on both measures for any algorithm; Section 5.1 says Balanced "fails to achieve better FE and MU-T". They find standard 1:1 sampling inefficient (little forgetting in 4 epochs), and cyclic sampling and MELU more stable. MELU beats cyclic notably under DPO (FE 0.70 to 0.82). They draw no conclusions about recovery attacks or about whether knowledge is hidden rather than removed.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies retain-set composition and sampling for GD, DPO, and NPO rather than testing the recovery attacks in the claim; it uses entity-unlearning data and FE/MU-T measures.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcomes vary with unlearning algorithm, retain-set composition, and sampling strategy.

fits_no_version.finding: After 4 epochs, standard 1:1 sampling (sequential or random) leaves FE at 0.32–0.37, against a 0.30 pre-unlearning baseline, for GD, DPO and NPO, with MU-T 0.71–0.74. Cyclic and MELU sampling reach FE 0.63–0.97 with MU-T 0.65–0.80. Footnote 6: DPO with 1:1 random sampling reaches FE 0.79 at 100 epochs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: How forget and retain samples are paired, and how many retain samples are used, strongly changes how much forgetting standard unlearning methods achieve on standard metrics, independent of any recovery attack.

fits_no_version.finding: With cyclic sampling, Indirect neighbours give higher MU-T than Direct for all three algorithms (GD 0.34 to 0.65, DPO 0.76 to 0.77, NPO 0.69 to 0.78). FE falls from Direct to Indirect for GD (0.96 to 0.89) and NPO (0.71 to 0.60) but rises for DPO (0.57 to 0.71). The Balanced mix is not better on both measures for any algorithm.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Which neighbour set makes up the retain set shifts unlearning's forget-efficacy/utility trade-off, in directions that differ by algorithm.

fits_no_version.finding: GD's high FE (0.89–0.97) comes with forget-set perplexity of about 1e82 to 1e90 (Table 1). The authors also report a sharp drop in forget-set token diversity, which they attribute to GD's degeneration behaviour.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: High forget-efficacy scores from gradient-difference unlearning can register degenerate output on forget queries rather than removal of the knowledge.

record.peer_reviewed: PKDD/ECML Workshops; preprint of chapter published in ECML PKDD 2025 Workshops, CCIS vol. 2840, Springer, 2026
record.problems: Only one model family and one model size are tested; only a few unlearning algorithms and batch unlearning are evaluated. Indirect-neighbor and test-set generation uses a sister model. The authors report no uncertainty estimates. FE is a composite metric, not direct accuracy relative to chance, and the study does not test post-unlearning recovery attacks.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted from the reported Table 1 sampling and data-practice FE/MU-T values. GA was not implemented according to Appendix A.3; MMLU and other appendix figures are not recorded as rows because they are ancillary general-utility or token-diversity measures rather than direct measures of the targeted-knowledge recovery in the claim.

untested.parts: Robustness of forgetting to any attack: no recovery attempt of any kind. Targeted-knowledge accuracy relative to chance is not measured (FE is a composite of ROUGE-L, probability and cosine on generations). The study measures standard-query forgetting and utility only, which cannot show whether the knowledge is gone.
No relearning or fine-tuning recovery after unlearning.
No activation-direction ablation and no analysis of whether access is blocked or the knowledge deleted.
No quantization of the unlearned models.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, other-language or in-context recovery.
No method is tested against recovery attacks. MELU is a sampling scheme assessed only on standard FE, MU-T, MMLU and token-diversity metrics.

record.verdict_notes: Repair of the quarantined Opus verdict. Changes: (1) The row ranges and lists ('r1, r2', 'r3-r20', 'r21-r26, ...', 'r27, ...') are expanded into 44 single-row items. (2) Every row carried the undeclared version V1. Each is relinked to none, decided from what it measures: standard-query FE or MU-T with no recovery attack, so none of A–F applies. All states are cannot_determine. (3) Both earlier 'missing' entries are removed. They bore on no version, and 'none' is not a declared identifier there. Their content now sits here and in fits_no_version. The removed facts are: Table 1 lists GA (FE 0.44, MU-T 0.67), plain DPO (0.70, 0.47) and plain NPO (0.30, 0.73) rows, although Appendix A.3 says GA was not implemented. The plain NPO row is identical to the pre-unlearning row in FE, MU-T and both perplexities, so it may be a copied baseline. The 100-epoch DPO footnote (FE 0.79, MU-T 0.78) is now in the first fits_no_version item. (4) The single fits_no_version finding is split into a sampling item and a retain-set-composition item, with complete row lists (the earlier list left out the MU-T rows and most data-practice rows). One new item is added on GD's high FE coinciding with degenerate output. (5) authors_conclusion now notes that the Balanced mix did not win in the authors' own table. The relation (uses_without_test), tranche (T4), test_reason, empty labels and the untested list are kept, with small wording edits. Other observations: the MMLU baseline of 12.42% is odd for LLaMA 3.1 8B Instruct (the paper cites MMLU-Pro, which has a 10% chance level). The test set Dt was included in the pre-unlearning fine-tuning (A.3). There is a single model, no uncertainty is reported, and the data-practice runs all use cyclic sampling (footnote 4). Read note: all prose, Table 1 and the figure captions were read; lines 2077–3599 of the text file are heatmap numbers extracted from figures, and a search found no prose there. The text contains no instructions to the reader.

versions.untested_parts: The study measures forget efficacy and test-set utility, but does not test whether targeted knowledge reaches chance-level accuracy or whether any simple attack recovers it.
No post-unlearning relearning or fine-tuning recovery set is used.
No activation-direction ablation or analysis of blocking access versus deleting knowledge is reported.
No low-bit quantization attack is tested.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, language variation, or in-context-information recovery test is reported.
No counter-method is evaluated for resistance to the recovery attacks in the claim.
